Suit
SOOT
n. (a set of garments; also a petition or legal cause)
From Old French suite, a following, from Latin sequi, to follow — things that go together, whether garments in a set or a cause pursued at law. The Authorized Version uses both senses.

Biblical Definition

The clothing sense appears in one of the strangest transactions in Scripture. Micah, a man of mount Ephraim with a house of gods and a homemade ephod, hires a wandering Levite: I will give thee ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in. A salary, a uniform, and board, and a priesthood purchased at a fixed rate. Micah's conclusion is one of the most self-deceived sentences in the Old Testament: Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest. He had broken the second commandment with the images, the regulative principle with the shrine, and the law of the priesthood with the appointment, and he read his own arrangement as a guarantee of blessing. The frame the book puts around it is the refrain of Judges: in those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes. The legal sense of the word appears in Absalom's campaign for the throne, promising justice to every man which hath any suit or cause, and in Job, where many shall make suit unto the restored man.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a set of things used together, as a suit of clothes; also, the prosecution of a claim, a petition, an entreaty.

expand to see more

SUIT, n. A set; a number of things used together, and in a degree necessary to be united; as a suit of clothes.

SUIT, n. The act of suing; the process by which one endeavors to gain an end or an object.

SUIT, n. Petition; entreaty; solicitation; a request made to a superior.

APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress.

HIRE, n. The price, reward or compensation paid for personal service.

Jdg 17:10 — "And Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father and a priest, and I will give thee ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in. a"

Jdg 17:6 — "In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

Jdg 17:13 — "Then said Micah, Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest."

2Sa 15:4 — "Absalom said moreover, Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!"

Modern Corruption

Worship is arranged according to what seems right and reverent to the worshipper, and its sincerity taken as its warrant; Judges 17 shows a devout man building exactly that and reading it as the LORD's favour.

expand to see more

Micah is not an atheist. He is religious, generous with silver, eager to have a Levite rather than his own son in the office, and convinced that God will do him good. Every element of his worship is invented and every element is sincere. This is precisely why the Reformed tradition holds the regulative principle: that what God has not commanded in his worship is not permitted, however devout the intention. Sincerity is not a warrant, and the second commandment forbids worshipping the true God by images of our own devising as firmly as it forbids false gods.

The refrain of the book supplies the diagnosis and it is political as well as religious: there was no king in Israel, and every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Where no authority is acknowledged, each man's conscience becomes his own liturgy committee, and Judges spends its closing chapters showing where that ends. A suit of apparel and ten shekels a year bought Micah a chaplain, and the Danites took chaplain, ephod, and images away from him by force a chapter later, which is the usual fate of a religion a man has made himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'erek beged (H6187, H899), an order or set of garments; riyb (H7379), a suit or cause at law; chalah (H2470), to entreat or make suit.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'erek (H6187) — an arrangement, an order, an estimate; with beged, a suit of apparel.

Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment, clothing; also treachery, from a root meaning to cover.

Hebrew riyb (H7379) — a contest, a controversy, a cause at law; any suit or cause.

Hebrew chalah (H2470) — to be weak, to entreat, to make suit; many shall make suit unto thee.

Hebrew yashar (H3477) — right, straight; right in his own eyes.

Usage

"“ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel” — a priesthood on salary."

"“every man which hath any suit or cause” — the legal sense, in Absalom's campaign."

"“Now know I that the LORD will do me good” — sincerity mistaken for warrant."
